Goneril. The eldest daughter of King Lear. She is a ruthless, ambitious woman who begins the play by falsely professing limitless love for her father. A flattery that wins her a third of his kingdom. She then systematically strips him of dignity, power, and comfort. She is motivated by a combination of pragmatism—she believes her father's age makes him obsolete—and passion. She lusts after Edmund, the bastard, and becomes her sister's rival. Her cruelty to her father initiates the tragic cascade, and her betrayals destroy the kingdom's ruling hierarchy.

When King Lear demands that his three daughters declare their love to determine how he divides his kingdom, Goneril and her sister Regan compete to make the most extravagant declarations. Goneril swears, "Sir, I love you more than words can wield the matter; Dearer than eye-sight, space, and liberty." The audience knows, and Goneril demonstrates, that this is a calculated lie designed to win her father's favor.

Once she has her portion of the kingdom, Goneril begins to reduce Lear's retinue—his armed followers. She argues that an old man has no need for a hundred knights. She orders her servants to be discourteous to him. She reduces his food. She refuses to greet him when he returns from hunting. Her actions are presented as pragmatic and also as personal cruelty. She enjoys humiliating him.

When Edmund enters the play as a possible ally, Goneril becomes obsessed with him. She writes him a love letter and promises him power. She is willing to betray her husband, the Duke of Albany, to be with Edmund. When Edmund is defeated in combat by Edgar, Goneril learns that her poison has killed Regan and that Edmund will not be able to marry her. She stabs herself, dying in a final act of frustrated passion and rage. Her suicide is not redemptive but a last assertion of her own will.

Goneril represents a woman who refuses the traditional feminine role of obedience and submission. She is ambitious, sexual, and willing to commit murder. Yet the play frames her ambition as monstrous. Her cruelty to her father is presented as unnatural, a violation of the natural order. Her death, and Regan's, restores a patriarchal order in which Edgar and Albany rule, without female power to disrupt them.
